categories.name: Prepare the Organization
categories.blurb: Make sure your people, processes, and tools are ready to develop software securely before any coding starts.

categories.name: Protect the Software
categories.blurb: Guard your code, releases, and their supporting data against tampering and unauthorized access throughout their life.

categories.name: Produce Well-Secured Software
categories.blurb: Design, build, and test software so that it has as few security weaknesses as possible when released.

categories.name: Respond to Vulnerabilities
categories.blurb: Find, fix, and learn from vulnerabilities in released software on an ongoing basis.

questions.text: Have you identified and written down the security requirements that govern your software development infrastructure and processes?
questions.why: Without documented security rules for how development happens, teams make inconsistent choices that leave gaps attackers exploit.
questions.fix: Draft a policy defining security requirements for your development environments, tools, and workflows.

questions.text: Have you identified and documented the security requirements that the software you build must meet?
questions.why: If security expectations for the product itself are undefined, they cannot be designed in, tested, or verified.
questions.fix: Write a baseline set of product security requirements covering areas like authentication, data protection, and logging.

questions.text: Do you communicate your security requirements to the third parties who supply commercial or open-source components you use?
questions.why: Suppliers who do not know your security expectations may deliver components that undermine your software's security.
questions.fix: Define a core set of supplier security requirements and share them in contracts or acquisition terms.

questions.text: Have you defined clear security roles and responsibilities for everyone involved in your software development lifecycle?
questions.why: When no one owns security tasks, critical work gets skipped and accountability disappears.
questions.fix: Document each SDLC role and assign specific security responsibilities to it.

questions.text: Do you provide role-based security training and ongoing education to the people who fill those development roles?
questions.why: Staff who lack security skills for their role introduce avoidable weaknesses no matter how good the process is.
questions.fix: Set up role-specific security training with defined learning outcomes and refresh it regularly.

questions.text: Has upper management committed to and provided resources for your secure software development program?
questions.why: Secure development efforts stall without leadership backing, budget, and clear authority to enforce them.
questions.fix: Appoint an accountable leader and secure a documented management commitment with resourcing.

questions.text: Have you specified which tools or tool types must be used across your development toolchains to reduce security risk?
questions.why: Ad-hoc tool choices create inconsistent coverage and leave security checks missing from parts of the pipeline.
questions.fix: Define toolchain categories and list the mandatory or recommended security tools for each.

questions.text: Do you follow recommended security practices when you deploy, operate, and maintain your development tools and toolchains?
questions.why: A poorly secured tool or pipeline becomes an attack path into your code and build outputs.
questions.fix: Evaluate the security of each tool before adoption and harden and patch it in operation.

questions.text: Are your tools configured to generate artifacts that show your secure development practices were actually followed?
questions.why: Without evidence from tooling you cannot prove, audit, or improve how well security practices are performed.
questions.fix: Enable logging and reporting in your tools to capture artifacts like scan results and approvals.

questions.text: Have you defined criteria that software must satisfy in security checks throughout the development lifecycle?
questions.why: Without pass or fail criteria, security reviews are subjective and insecure software can ship unchallenged.
questions.fix: Write measurable security acceptance criteria and gate points for each phase of the SDLC.

questions.text: Do you have processes and mechanisms that gather and safeguard the information needed to judge those security criteria?
questions.why: Security decisions based on missing or unreliable data lead to false confidence and overlooked risk.
questions.fix: Automate collection of security evidence from your toolchain and store it with integrity protection.

questions.text: Do you separate and protect each of your development, build, test, and related environments from one another?
questions.why: A compromise in one environment can spread to production or build systems if they are not isolated.
questions.fix: Segment environments with access controls and use strong risk-based authentication between them.

questions.text: Do you secure and harden the endpoints, such as developer workstations, that are used for software development?
questions.why: A compromised developer machine gives attackers direct access to source code, credentials, and the pipeline.
questions.fix: Apply an approved hardening baseline and endpoint protection to every development device.

questions.text: Do you store all forms of code, including source and configuration-as-code, with controls that block unauthorized access and changes?
questions.why: Unprotected code can be stolen or tampered with, injecting backdoors before anyone notices.
questions.fix: Keep all code in an access-controlled repository and require authenticated, logged changes.

questions.text: Do you give users a way to verify that a software release is authentic and has not been altered?
questions.why: Without an integrity check, users cannot tell a genuine release from a tampered or malicious copy.
questions.fix: Publish cryptographic hashes or digital signatures for every release on a trusted channel.

questions.text: Do you securely archive the files and data needed to be retained for each software release?
questions.why: If release artifacts are lost or altered you cannot investigate incidents, reproduce builds, or support the software.
questions.fix: Store release files and images in protected, access-controlled repositories with integrity safeguards.

questions.text: Do you collect and safeguard provenance data, such as a software bill of materials, for each release and share it as needed?
questions.why: Without provenance and component data you cannot quickly assess exposure when a dependency is found vulnerable.
questions.fix: Generate an SBOM for each release and make it available to acquirers and internal teams.

questions.text: Do you use risk modeling, such as threat modeling or attack surface analysis, to assess the security risks in your software?
questions.why: Design flaws missed early are the most expensive and dangerous weaknesses to fix later.
questions.fix: Run a threat modeling session on each significant feature and record the risks it surfaces.

questions.text: Do you track and maintain the software's security requirements, risks, and design decisions over time?
questions.why: Untracked security decisions get lost, reversed, or contradicted as the software evolves.
questions.fix: Record each security risk and its planned mitigation in a living, reviewable document.

questions.text: Where appropriate, do you build in support for using standard security features and services instead of custom-built ones?
questions.why: Home-grown security mechanisms are far more likely to contain flaws than vetted standard ones.
questions.fix: Adopt proven libraries and services for functions like authentication, encryption, and logging.

questions.text: Do qualified reviewers check the software design to confirm it meets your security requirements and addresses known risks?
questions.why: A design that does not satisfy security requirements will produce insecure software no matter how well it is coded.
questions.fix: Have a qualified person review each design against the security requirements and risk information.

questions.text: Do you acquire and maintain well-secured third-party software components rather than building everything from scratch?
questions.why: Reusing vetted components reduces the chance of introducing new flaws in code you would otherwise write yourself.
questions.fix: Evaluate third-party components for security in context before reuse and keep them updated.

questions.text: Do you create and maintain your own reusable software components following secure practices?
questions.why: Insecure shared components multiply a single weakness across every product that reuses them.
questions.fix: Apply your secure design and coding standards when building internal reusable modules.

questions.text: Do you verify that acquired commercial, open-source, and other third-party components meet your security requirements?
questions.why: Unverified dependencies can carry known vulnerabilities straight into your product.
questions.fix: Continuously scan components for known vulnerabilities and confirm they meet your requirements.

questions.text: Do your developers follow established secure coding practices, such as input validation and output encoding, when writing code?
questions.why: Most common vulnerabilities come from insecure coding patterns that secure practices would prevent.
questions.fix: Adopt a secure coding standard and validate all inputs and encode all outputs by default.

questions.text: Do you use compilers, interpreters, and build tools that provide security features, kept at up-to-date versions?
questions.why: Outdated or feature-poor build tools miss protections that could catch or block whole classes of bugs.
questions.fix: Standardize on current toolchain versions that offer built-in security features.

questions.text: Have you determined and enabled the compiler, interpreter, and build settings that improve the security of your software?
questions.why: Security hardening flags and warnings do nothing to protect you if they are left turned off.
questions.fix: Turn on security warnings and hardening options like stack protections in your build configuration.

questions.text: Have you decided when code review or code analysis should be performed and defined how it will be done?
questions.why: Without a defined review policy, code inspection happens inconsistently and misses defects.
questions.fix: Write a policy stating when peer review and automated analysis are required for code changes.

questions.text: Do you actually perform the code review and code analysis according to your defined process?
questions.why: A review policy that is not followed leaves the same defects it was meant to catch.
questions.fix: Run peer review and static analysis on changes and require findings to be resolved before merge.

questions.text: Have you decided when executable code testing should be performed and defined how it will be done?
questions.why: Some vulnerabilities only appear at runtime, so undefined testing lets them reach production.
questions.fix: Establish a policy for when dynamic testing, fuzzing, or penetration testing is required.

questions.text: Do you scope, design, and carry out testing of the running software to find security weaknesses?
questions.why: Runtime flaws that are never exercised in testing become the vulnerabilities attackers find first.
questions.fix: Perform functional and negative security testing of running builds, including fuzzing where relevant.

questions.text: Have you defined a secure baseline for the software's default configuration settings?
questions.why: Insecure defaults leave most users exposed because few ever change the shipped settings.
questions.fix: Determine and document the most secure practical default configuration for the software.

questions.text: Do you implement those secure defaults so the software ships in its hardened configuration?
questions.why: A secure baseline that is defined but not applied gives users no real protection out of the box.
questions.fix: Set the approved secure settings as the shipped defaults and verify them before release.

questions.text: Do you actively gather information about potential vulnerabilities in your software from users, databases, and other sources?
questions.why: Vulnerabilities you never hear about remain unpatched and open to exploitation.
questions.fix: Monitor vulnerability databases, security mailing lists, and reports for issues affecting your software.

questions.text: Do you review, analyze, or test your software to identify and confirm vulnerabilities and judge their severity?
questions.why: Unconfirmed or unranked reports make it impossible to respond to the most dangerous issues first.
questions.fix: Use automated analysis and testing to confirm reported vulnerabilities and assess their severity.

questions.text: Do you have a vulnerability disclosure policy that makes it easy for outsiders to report security issues to you?
questions.why: Without an easy reporting channel, finders may disclose flaws publicly or sell them instead of telling you.
questions.fix: Publish a vulnerability disclosure policy with a clear contact and intake process.

questions.text: Do you analyze each vulnerability thoroughly enough to gather the information needed to plan a response?
questions.why: Responding without understanding a vulnerability's scope leads to incomplete or wrong fixes.
questions.fix: Record and analyze each vulnerability in your issue tracker to understand its cause and impact.

questions.text: Do you plan and carry out appropriate risk responses, such as remediation, for the vulnerabilities you confirm?
questions.why: Confirmed vulnerabilities that are never remediated stay exploitable in the field.
questions.fix: Make a risk-based decision for each vulnerability and implement and ship the chosen fix.

questions.text: Do you analyze confirmed vulnerabilities to determine their underlying root causes?
questions.why: Fixing only the symptom leaves the root cause free to produce the same flaw again.
questions.fix: Perform root cause analysis on discovered vulnerabilities and record what you find.

questions.text: Do you review root causes over time to spot recurring patterns across your vulnerabilities?
questions.why: Recurring patterns signal systemic process gaps that keep generating new vulnerabilities.
questions.fix: Aggregate root cause findings and review trends to identify systemic weaknesses to address.

questions.text: Do you proactively review your software for other vulnerabilities similar to ones you have already found?
questions.why: The same class of flaw often appears in many places, so fixing one instance leaves the rest exploitable.
questions.fix: Search the codebase for other instances of each confirmed flaw and remediate them too.

questions.text: Do you review and update your software development process based on lessons learned from vulnerabilities?
questions.why: If the process that produced a vulnerability never changes, it will keep producing similar ones.
questions.fix: Feed root cause lessons back into your SDLC and update practices to prevent recurrence.
